human_interpretation_en.heading: Nothing comes from one cause, and the same thing helps in more than one way
human_interpretation_en.text: Both books insist that nothing arises from a single cause. Margaya's example is a match and its box. The chemical on the match-head and the chemical on the side of the box both help make the flame, but in different ways. If they helped in the same way, either one would be enough. The method is less about how things are connected and more about how, exactly, each one helps. One thing can hold something steady, give it something to rest on, go before it, come after it, feed it, or step out of the way so something else can take its place. Asking 'in what way does this help?' is a sharper question than 'what caused this?'.

human_interpretation_en.heading: What we look back on can feed very different things
human_interpretation_en.text: Pradeepika spends much of this section on a simple observation. Someone gives a gift or keeps a promise, and later thinks about it. That memory can bring quiet gladness. It can just as easily bring pride ('I did something great'), possessiveness ('my good deed'), doubt ('was it really good?'), restlessness, or regret. The act stays the same. What changes is the state of mind that takes it up. The reverse is also true. A past flash of anger or greed, looked at honestly, can support clear seeing rather than more of the same. On this view a person's history is not fixed in its effects. It keeps being used as raw material by whatever state of mind picks it up now.

human_interpretation_en.heading: Some support makes, some support only keeps going, and absence can help too
human_interpretation_en.text: The sources separate help that produces something from help that only sustains what is already there. Roots do both: they give rise to steadiness and keep it steady. In Margaya, some later things only support what came before, without producing it. Food keeps a life going long after it began. Most strikingly, the ending of one moment is counted as a real help, because it clears the space the next moment needs. So help here includes going away, not only being present.

human_interpretation_en.heading: What we hold in high regard quietly steers us
human_interpretation_en.text: The text describes something anyone can recognise: when we truly value something, whether a person, a memory, a skill or a past good act, it keeps drawing the mind back and bends our present choices towards it, the way a gem once seen keeps returning to thought. The same valued thing can be held in two very different ways. We can admire it for what is genuinely good in it, or we can cling to it because it tastes pleasant, and then admiration turns into pride of ownership: 'my good deed'. The source is blunt about this. Even generosity, remembered with self-satisfaction, can feed greed and a fixed view of oneself.

human_interpretation_en.heading: Only one voice leads at a time
human_interpretation_en.text: When we act, several forces are present together: wanting to do it, the mind's own drive, sheer effort, and careful testing. The text says only one of them takes the lead at any moment, and only when it is strong. Everything else lines up behind it. This is a precise, modest claim. It does not say willpower conquers all. It says that in each moment of action something leads and the rest follows, and that the leader can change.

human_interpretation_en.heading: Each moment hands over to the next
human_interpretation_en.text: Experience is not one continuous thing. It is a relay in which each moment, as it ends, makes room for the next and passes on its momentum with no gap in between. The source adds a striking detail: even after a long stretch in which nothing is experienced at all, the last moment before the gap still connects directly to the first moment after it. Continuity does not depend on unbroken time. It depends on handing over. The text also marks where the relay stops, with one final moment that has no successor.

human_interpretation_en.heading: Nothing arises alone
human_interpretation_en.text: Nothing, whether a feeling, a thought or a lump of matter, comes into being on its own. Things arise in clusters, and each member of the cluster helps the others exist, sometimes in both directions and sometimes in one only. Feeling, perception, intention and awareness hold each other up. The basic qualities of matter hold each other up and carry everything built on them. For a group whose question is what changes when we see that nothing, including ourselves, stands alone, this is the most direct statement in this part of the text.

human_interpretation_en.heading: Some things stand only by leaning on each other
human_interpretation_en.text: The first idea here is simple and physical. Some parts of an experience hold each other up in the same instant, the way three poles stay upright only when they lean together. Pull one away and the others fall. The text is careful about this, though. Many things that appear together do not hold each other up equally. Some support runs in only one direction: the mind moves the body, but that movement does not hold the mind up in return. 'Everything supports everything' is exactly the claim the text avoids.

human_interpretation_en.heading: What you stand on was already there
human_interpretation_en.text: The second idea is about ground. Every experience rests on something, sometimes on what arises alongside it and sometimes on what was already in place: an eye before seeing, a body before feeling. The text follows this even to the last moments of a life, when the body that has carried a person is also the thing the dying mind turns towards. What came first becomes the floor for what comes next.

human_interpretation_en.heading: The strongest reasons are the ones we have fed
human_interpretation_en.text: The third idea gets the most space in this part. The heaviest influence on what someone thinks or does next is not just what is in front of them. It is what they have honoured, what happened a moment before, and above all what they have practised again and again. The direction is not tidy. Faith, learning and generosity can quietly feed pride and a sense of being better than others. A wrong someone has done can push them towards giving and repair. Warm weather or harsh weather, a good meal or a poor one, a dry bed or a leaking roof can tip a day towards patience or towards cruelty. This is a picture of people shaped by many strong pressures, some chosen and some not, and none of them decides the outcome alone.

human_interpretation_en.heading: Support runs both ways in time
human_interpretation_en.text: The text's two images belong together. A tree that grew first holds up the flowers and fruit that come later. And the rain and weather that come later keep that same tree alive. What is already standing makes the next thing possible: the eye has to exist, and the thing seen has to be there, before seeing can happen. But what comes later also keeps the earlier thing going: the text says the ongoing activity of the mind keeps the body's continuity from breaking. Nothing here is only a cause or only an effect. Each thing leans on what came before it and is held up by what comes after it.

human_interpretation_en.heading: The same thing, two directions
human_interpretation_en.text: The same physical eye, or the same sound, can support very different mental events. A person can look at their own body and see clearly that it is fragile and passing. Or they can enjoy it, crave it, worry about it or feel aversion. The thing itself stays neutral. What grows from it depends on what meets it. The source shows this point case by case, so it is less a moral than a careful map of how one ordinary object can lead to calm or to trouble.

human_interpretation_en.heading: An act has two lives
human_interpretation_en.text: An intention does two jobs. In the moment, it organises everything happening with it, including the body's movement. It can also leave behind a capacity that ripens much later, in a different moment entirely. The results that ripen are described as quiet and passive: they cannot act or push. This separates the energy of choosing from the stillness of what one receives. Repetition works in a similar way, but on a far shorter scale: each moment of the same kind gives force to the next, whether that kind is generous or harmful.

human_interpretation_en.heading: What keeps a life going
human_interpretation_en.text: Food keeps a body going, and the text says three less obvious things 'feed' a life just as much: contact with the world, intention and awareness. It describes the pleasure of contact as the thing that stops people from growing weary of the whole cycle. Alongside these, certain capacities act like governors: life, attention, effort, mindfulness, understanding, and the senses themselves each keep what depends on them working within their own domain. The body is sustained by food and weather, and the mind by what it touches, wants and knows.

human_interpretation_en.heading: Some kinds of help steer
human_interpretation_en.text: Two of the supports here are about direction rather than presence. One is the way close attention grips something and pulls everything else in the moment along with it. The other is a set of tendencies that point a person down a road. The source is plain that both work in either direction: the same gripping attention runs in a moment of greed as in a moment of care, and alongside the eight 'right' ways there are four 'wrong' ones (wrong view, wrong intention, wrong effort, wrong concentration) that are just as effective at steering. Being focused and having direction are not virtues in themselves. What matters is where they point.

human_interpretation_en.heading: Help that merges, and help that stays separate
human_interpretation_en.text: Some things only make sense together. They start together, end together, face the same thing and rest on the same ground, like the several strands of a single moment of feeling and knowing. Other things hold each other up while staying distinct, as the body and the mind do, or the eye and the seeing. The teaching carefully keeps these two kinds of support apart: closeness is not the only way to hold something up, and some of the most important support happens between things that never mix.

human_interpretation_en.heading: Being there, and getting out of the way
human_interpretation_en.text: One thing can help another simply by still being there, as the four basic elements of matter keep each other in place. A thing can also help by ending: a moment of mind has to finish before the next can arise, and that clearing-away counts as a real contribution rather than a loss. The text names both twice over (present / not gone, absent / gone) so that neither side is forgotten. Staying and leaving are both ways of supporting what comes next.

human_interpretation_en.heading: A map, not a slogan
human_interpretation_en.text: The part closes with a table that sorts all twenty-four kinds of support by whether they are mental or physical, whether they act from the past, the present, the future or outside time, whether they bring something into being or only keep it going, and in what kind of life they operate. The point is precision: 'things depend on each other' is only the start, and the useful question is how, when and in which direction.

does_not_transfer: 'Everything is connected' is too loose. The source is exact and bounded. It says which things support which, in which of twenty-four specific ways, and (in Pradeepika) explicitly lists what a given condition does NOT support. It also holds that nibbāna and concepts can support without themselves being conditioned.

It is not a theory of ecology, social networks or physical cause and effect. Its subject is momentary mental events and material events in a living being. The match-and-box image is an analogy, not the doctrine itself.
It is not 'think good thoughts and good things follow'. The same good deed, recalled, can feed craving, conceit or regret. The object does not settle what arises; the mind that takes it up does.

The six 'roots' are not the same as modern 'motives' or personality traits. They are moment-by-moment factors that fix the mind on its object, and the text treats them as present or absent in each moment.

The worked examples involving supernormal knowledges (reading others' minds, recalling past lives) and the traditional account of rays from the Buddha's body in the fourth week are devotional or technical material. They should not be restated as factual claims in a film, and should not be mocked.

'Everything is connected' is too loose. Co-nascence in the source is specific: states arising at the same moment in one cluster, with defined directions of support. Mind-born matter, for example, is only supported and does not support back [C082-P:L2822].

Predominance is not a 'leadership' or 'willpower wins' message. Only one of four factors leads at a time, only when strong, and the text names desire-to-act, mind, energy and investigation, not personality or authority [C082-P:L1740].
'Honour your good deeds' is not a safe slogan here. The source shows that revering one's own merit can become the object of greed and of the view 'my merit' [C082-P:L1723–L1727] [C082-P:L1880–L1888].

Proximity and contiguity are not 'life goes on' or the continuity of a self. They describe moment-to-moment succession of mental states only, and the relay ends with an arahant's final death-moment [C082-P:L2220] [C082-P:L2226].
The four great elements named here (paṭhavī, āpo, tejo, vāyo) should not be flattened into modern chemistry or into literal soil, water, fire and wind. This part names them without defining them.

'Everything is connected' distorts it. The text maps specific, directional relations and says outright that some things that arise together do not support each other (mind-born matter does not support the mind in return; derived matter does not support other derived matter) [C082-P:L3346], [C082-P:L3616].
Mutuality is not a picture of social cooperation or community mutual aid. In the source it describes states and elements inside a single moment of experience, not people helping each other.

'Good things only come from good things' is contradicted. The source shows wholesome states giving strong support to conceit and wrong view, and unwholesome states giving strong support to giving and practice. Its one fixed limit is that the highest wholesome state cannot support the unwholesome [C082-P:L4947].

'Your environment determines you' is too strong. Weather, food, lodging and bodily comfort are strong supports, but for both good and bad outcomes. They are not sole causes [C082-P:L5623–L5643], [C082-P:L5697–L5719].

The passages on the five gravest acts and fixed wrong view leading to hell are doctrinal claims about outcomes after death [C082-P:L5285], [C082-P:L5289]. They must not become a moral threat or a verdict on anyone who appears on screen.
'Even wanting enlightenment is just another desire' is a popular slogan the text rejects: aspiration for the end of suffering is classed as wholesome aspiration, not craving [C082-P:L4949].

'You reap what you sow' as cosmic justice: the source's kamma condition is technical. A past volition conditions specific resultant mental states and kamma-born matter, and those results are described as inert and quiet, not as reward or punishment [C082-P:L6357–L6367; L6721].

'Practice makes perfect': repetition (āsevana) here works between split-second impulsion moments of the same kind and feeling. It is not skill built up over years, and it strengthens unwholesome series as much as wholesome ones [C082-P:L6159; L6283–L6301].

'Food for the soul': the source does not present the nutriment of contact as healthy nourishment. It says delight in felt experience keeps beings from tiring of the round of rebirth, which is not a wellness message [C082-P:L6874].
'Mind over body' or 'the mind heals the body': postnascence only says later mental states support body matter that already exists. It makes no therapeutic claim [C082-P:L6055; L6065].

Faculty (indriya) as 'willpower' or self-control: the source means each governing state leads within its own function. It also explicitly excludes the femininity and masculinity faculties as conditions, so this should not become a slogan about gender [C082-P:L7124–L7128].

'Everything is connected' is too loose. Each condition names exactly which states support which, and lists 'excluded' states that a given kind of support does not reach (e.g. all matter is excluded from association support, L7831–L7833).

'Just being present is a gift': the presence condition is technical. It covers the four elements holding each other, the eye base, nutriment and so on, and it also supports craving (delighting in the eye gives rise to lust, L8712–L8722). It is not an emotional or moral claim about showing up for people.

'Letting go makes room for the new' borrows the absence condition too loosely. The source is about one mind-moment ceasing so the next can arise in a strict one-at-a-time sequence, not about life choices or decluttering.
'Focus and flow are good for you': absorption factors and path factors work in unwholesome minds too, and the path condition explicitly includes four wrong path factors.
'Presence is universal existence': the text says outright that nibbāna is not a presence condition (L8246), so the idea should not be stretched into a metaphysics of all-pervading being.

story_seeds.seed: A family prepares a large almsgiving meal for a death anniversary, relying on many people who each help in a different way
story_seeds.what_camera_could_observe: Firewood arriving, borrowed pots, a neighbour who only grinds coconut, another who only keeps the fire going, the order in which things must happen, and the quiet after the monks leave, when people talk about how it went.
story_seeds.why_it_fits: It shows one outcome needing many different kinds of help. The talk afterwards shows that one act of giving, looked back on, can bring gladness, pride, worry or regret. That is the object condition as Pradeepika illustrates it.
story_seeds.setting_type: a rural or small-town Sri Lankan household preparing a dāna
story_seeds.risk: The family's grief could become a prop for doctrine. The film could stage 'reflective' moments. It could also nudge people towards pride or regret for the camera. It needs clear consent and a light touch.

story_seeds.seed: A potter's kiln firing that depends on fuel, weather, clay and someone staying awake through the night
story_seeds.what_camera_could_observe: Loading the kiln, choosing the wood, watching the wind, feeding the fire at intervals through the night, the moment the kiln is opened, and which pots survived.
story_seeds.why_it_fits: Like Margaya's match and box, the fire needs several things that each help differently. Some things produce the heat and some only keep it going. Timing matters too: what must be there before, and what only helps afterwards.
story_seeds.setting_type: a traditional pottery village or small kiln workshop
story_seeds.risk: Turning craft into a neat metaphor, or over-narrating the doctrine on top of real work. It must be worth watching as a night of labour first.

story_seeds.seed: Farmers sharing water from one village tank on a rotation of turns
story_seeds.what_camera_could_observe: The sluice being opened, water moving field to field, who gets water when, one channel being closed so another can fill, and conversations at the tank bund about timing.
story_seeds.why_it_fits: One source supports many fields in sequence. The closing of one channel is what lets another fill, which is close to the idea that an absence or departure can itself be a help. What happens upstream earlier supports what happens downstream later.
story_seeds.setting_type: a dry-zone village irrigated from a small tank
story_seeds.risk: Water disputes are real and sensitive. The film must not sharpen conflict for drama, or reduce farmers' livelihoods to an illustration.

story_seeds.seed: An elderly craftsman returns to see a piece of work he made decades ago
story_seeds.what_camera_could_observe: Him seeing the carving or structure again, touching it, noticing repairs others have made, and what he says or leaves unsaid.
story_seeds.why_it_fits: A past act becomes the object of a present mind. Whether it brings contentment, pride, attachment ('my work') or regret depends on how he takes it up, which is Pradeepika's point about looking back.
story_seeds.setting_type: a village temple, old house or public building where local craftsmen worked
story_seeds.risk: Steering him towards a 'moving' reaction, staging the return, or turning an old man's memory into a lesson.

story_seeds.seed: A family preparing its yearly almsgiving for a departed elder, retelling how earlier ones were done
story_seeds.what_camera_could_observe: Days of preparation: cooking, borrowing vessels, inviting monks; elders taking out old photographs of past almsgivings and explaining 'how we have always done it'; the small tensions over doing it properly; the morning itself and the quiet afterwards.
story_seeds.why_it_fits: The source's own example of predominance: a past good act, remembered with reverence, becomes the object that steers present minds. The same act can also be held with pride of ownership [C082-P:L1808–L1818] [C082-P:L1880–L1886]. The film only has to watch how a remembered act shapes present behaviour.
story_seeds.setting_type: a family home in a rural village and its nearby temple
story_seeds.risk: Judging the family's devotion or pride; intruding on grief; turning a religious observance into a thesis. It needs full consent and a non-evaluative eye.

story_seeds.seed: A shift handover in a small railway signal cabin, where nothing may be left in the gap
story_seeds.what_camera_could_observe: The outgoing keeper briefing the incoming one: the logbook, the lever positions, the next train's timing; the moment responsibility passes; the new keeper's first act.
story_seeds.why_it_fits: An outward echo of proximity: the preceding moment gives way and makes the next possible with no gap [C082-P:L2220] [C082-P:L2224]. This is an analogy only. The source is about moments of mind, not about people.
story_seeds.setting_type: a rural railway station or level crossing
story_seeds.risk: Aestheticising routine labour; implying workers are 'illustrations'; safety rules may restrict filming.

story_seeds.seed: A young learner of traditional drumming preparing for a first public performance
story_seeds.what_camera_could_observe: Weeks of practice: days of eager wanting, days of grinding repetition, days of slow, careful correction by a teacher; the performance itself.
story_seeds.why_it_fits: Co-nascent predominance: wanting, mind, effort and investigation are all present, but one leads at a time and only when strong [C082-P:L1731–L1740]. A camera can see which one seems to be leading, without anyone naming it.
story_seeds.setting_type: a village drumming teacher's practice space
story_seeds.risk: Forcing a fourfold template onto a real person; narrating inner states the camera cannot see.

story_seeds.seed: A potter's workshop where a pot exists only when clay, water, fire and drying air all come together
story_seeds.what_camera_could_observe: Kneading clay, throwing on the wheel, drying in shade and breeze, firing the kiln, and the pots that crack when one part fails.
story_seeds.why_it_fits: Co-nascence: nothing arises alone, and the great elements in any bit of matter support one another and what is built on them [C082-P:L2816–L2822] [C082-P:L3196–L3208]. This is a visual echo, not a literal illustration: the source's elements are not clay or kilns.
story_seeds.setting_type: a traditional pottery village
story_seeds.risk: Making it a physics lesson; presenting craftspeople as quaint; the metaphor overpowering the potter's own story.

story_seeds.seed: A crew raising a tall temporary festival frame from bamboo or timber poles that only stays up once the poles are lashed and leaning together.
story_seeds.what_camera_could_observe: Poles steadied by hand, the moment the frame first holds without anyone touching it, a pole taken out and the whole structure shifting, and the same frame taken down after the festival.
story_seeds.why_it_fits: It shows the text's own image of mutual support: sticks that stand only by leaning on one another [C082-P:L3346]. It also shows that the finished decorations hang from the frame and do not hold it up, which matches the one-way support the text describes.
story_seeds.setting_type: A village temple ground or roadside during a seasonal festival.
story_seeds.risk: It could turn into a neat visual metaphor with a voice-over lecture. The film has to be about the builders, their skill and their deadline, and not use the frame as a diagram.

story_seeds.seed: A household or village group preparing a large act of giving, such as a roadside free-food stall during a festival, over several days.
story_seeds.what_camera_could_observe: Planning, cooking and serving, and the quieter moments around them: people comparing their stall with the next one, counting who came, feeling proud, and talking about why they do it every year.
story_seeds.why_it_fits: The source says generosity and faith can decisively support more generosity, but can also support pride and a feeling of superiority [C082-P:L4913–L4945]. A long observation can hold both without judging.
story_seeds.setting_type: A village or small-town road during a religious festival season.
story_seeds.risk: It could expose or mock people's pride. Participants must not be framed as hypocrites, and any edit that makes their generosity look fake should be avoided.

story_seeds.seed: A family or small community living through a hard monsoon stretch, where weather, food and a dry place to sleep visibly shape the mood of the days.
story_seeds.what_camera_could_observe: Rain days and clear days, what is cooked when supplies run low, people sharing or quarrelling over dry space, and kindness or short tempers changing with the weather.
story_seeds.why_it_fits: The text names weather, food, lodging and bodily comfort or pain as strong supports for both wholesome and unwholesome states [C082-P:L5509–L5527], [C082-P:L5697–L5719].
story_seeds.setting_type: A coastal fishing settlement or a hill-country estate community during the monsoon.
story_seeds.risk: It could become poverty as spectacle, or show hardship without consent. People must keep control over what is shown, and the film should not suggest that their circumstances decide their character.

story_seeds.seed: Someone who chose, after a past mistake they are willing to talk about, to spend years in steady service, such as volunteering at a care home or helping to rebuild something.
story_seeds.what_camera_could_observe: The daily routine of the service, the repetition, how others relate to the person, and their own account, in their own words, of what started it.
story_seeds.why_it_fits: The source describes a wrong done becoming a strong support for giving and discipline undertaken to counter it [C082-P:L5337–L5353], and describes repeated practice as decisive support [C082-P:L4359].
story_seeds.setting_type: A care facility, community workshop or rebuilding site in an ordinary town.
story_seeds.risk: It depends on the person freely choosing to share a private past. It must never be staged, pushed or framed as redemption theatre, and the past wrong should not be dramatised.

story_seeds.seed: A household that still waters and tends a tree planted by a grandparent before any of the present family was born.
story_seeds.what_camera_could_observe: Morning watering, clearing leaves, the tree's flowering or fruiting season, family members using its shade or fruit, the weather over a year.
story_seeds.why_it_fits: It mirrors the source's own images: the earlier tree supports later flowers and fruit (prenascence), and later water and weather keep the earlier tree alive (postnascence).
story_seeds.setting_type: Home garden or temple yard in a rural village
story_seeds.risk: It could turn into a literal picture of the simile. The film should follow the family's own reasons for tending the tree, not force a lesson onto it.

story_seeds.seed: A traditional drumming or dance teacher running a practice session where one rhythm is repeated until it takes hold.
story_seeds.what_camera_could_observe: The same phrase played again and again, and the moment a student's playing gains force and settles into its pattern within one session.
story_seeds.why_it_fits: It is a loose, visible echo of repetition: each repetition of the same kind strengthens the next.
story_seeds.setting_type: Village practice hall or a teacher's home verandah
story_seeds.risk: It could collapse into 'practice makes perfect', which the source does not teach, because repetition in the source works at the level of moments. Treat it as an echo, not an illustration.

story_seeds.seed: A family preparing and serving a large alms meal, from the intention and the early cooking through to the giving.
story_seeds.what_camera_could_observe: Planning, cooking before dawn, the work people share out, the act of giving, and the tiredness and quiet afterwards.
story_seeds.why_it_fits: The source's own example of volition is giving. The intention shapes the work as it happens (conascent kamma). Any later ripening cannot be filmed, and the film should say so honestly.
story_seeds.setting_type: Village household and a nearby temple on an alms-giving day
story_seeds.risk: It could slide into promoting merit, or claim future results that nobody can show. Stay with the effort and the relationships the camera can actually see.

story_seeds.seed: A kitchen that feeds many workers during a harvest or a long communal task.
story_seeds.what_camera_could_observe: Cooking in bulk, meal breaks, food carried out to the fields, and the energy of the work before and after eating.
story_seeds.why_it_fits: Edible food sustaining bodies that then carry on working is the plainest, most observable form of the nutriment condition.
story_seeds.setting_type: Paddy-field village during harvest, or a community work site
story_seeds.risk: Filming scarcity or hunger without care could be exploitative. The meal should be seen as shared labour and dignity, not deprivation.

story_seeds.seed: A beach-seine crew hauling a net from the shore, where no single pull does anything until everyone pulls at the same time
story_seeds.what_camera_could_observe: Two lines of people leaning back in rhythm, the call that sets the timing, the moment the pull falls out of step and the net stalls, the shared catch sorted on the sand
story_seeds.why_it_fits: Echoes association support: several parts that arise together, face one object and end together, each helping the others only because they are joined in one act. The fit is an analogy only; the source is about mental states within one moment.
story_seeds.setting_type: Open sandy coast used for shore-seine fishing
story_seeds.risk: Turning working people into a tidy metaphor; romanticising hard, low-paid labour; implying the crew illustrate a doctrine they never chose to speak about.

story_seeds.seed: A dawn shift change at a factory or harbour, where one crew has to clear the floor before the next can take over the same machines
story_seeds.what_camera_could_observe: Workers handing over, stepping away, the brief empty moment at a station, the next person stepping in to the same spot and continuing
story_seeds.why_it_fits: Echoes the absence and disappearance conditions: the leaving is what makes room. Honest caveat: the source concerns mind-moments that strictly follow one another, not people.
story_seeds.setting_type: Tea factory, fish harbour or other continuous-shift workplace
story_seeds.risk: Too neat a metaphor; filming in workplaces without management pressure shaping who appears; flattening workers' own stories into 'handover' symbolism.

story_seeds.seed: An elderly craftsperson who no longer works at the bench but still sits in the workshop while younger family members carry on
story_seeds.what_camera_could_observe: The younger makers glancing over, adjusting, asking a question or not asking; how the rhythm of work changes on days the elder is and is not there
story_seeds.why_it_fits: Echoes the presence and non-disappearance conditions: support simply by still being there, and being 'not yet gone'. It must stay observational, and the change may turn out to be small or absent.
story_seeds.setting_type: Family-run workshop in a craft village (pottery, brass, weaving, mask carving)
story_seeds.risk: Projecting meaning onto an elder's silence; framing age or decline sentimentally; staging 'absent' days.

story_seeds.seed: A young apprentice learning a precise craft, where the whole task depends on attention locking onto one small thing
story_seeds.what_camera_could_observe: Hands and eyes on a gem facet, a carving line or a drum skin; the moment attention slips and the work goes wrong; the master's correction
story_seeds.why_it_fits: Echoes the absorption condition: attention that goes to, enters and examines the object carries everything else in that moment with it. The source also says the same gripping works in unwholesome states, so the film should not present focus as automatically good.
story_seeds.setting_type: Small craft workshop or teaching household
story_seeds.risk: Treating concentration as mystical; slipping into a 'mindfulness' lecture; slowing the film down to make a doctrinal point.

cross_source_notes: Both sources list the same twenty-four conditions in the same order and treat the Pali list as the base text. Margaya asks the student to memorise it (M L11–L13) and gives Sinhala forms such as අන්‍යොන්‍ය, නිශ්ශ්‍රය and පශ්චාජ්ජාත (M L15–L40). Pradeepika keeps the Pali names and adds a one-line gloss for each (P L37–L87).
They agree that there is no dhamma without some condition-power, and that nibbāna and concepts are conditions but not conditioned (P L91–L95; M L7).
Pradeepika places the Paṭṭhāna as the detailed third tier of the teaching on cause and effect, after the four truths and the twelve-link chain (P L25–L29). Margaya does not make this framing.

Margaya illustrates condition-power with the match and matchbox (M L3–L5). Pradeepika illustrates the one-thing-many-ways point with greed as root, object, predominance and so on (P L97). Both use the tree-root simile for the root condition (P L107; M L46).
Pradeepika adds a third category, paccanīka (what is excluded), and analyses each condition as a 'three-set' (P L101, L145–L179). Margaya uses only condition and conditioned.

Pradeepika sets out the canonical answer patterns (7 for root, 9 for object) with long worked thought-process examples (P L183–L1633). Margaya has no such patterns and instead gives a compact definition of all 24 conditions (M L44–L200).

On the root condition both give the same conditioned set: 71 rooted consciousnesses, the 52 mental factors minus the delusion of the delusion-rooted mind, and rooted mind-born and rebirth kamma-born matter. Both note that delusion in the delusion-rooted mind is a condition only (P L121, L163–L166; M L46–L48).
Both give seven co-present strengths for an unwholesome root (hetu, sahajāta, aññamañña, nissaya, sampayutta, atthi, avigata) (P L274; M L206).

The glosses differ. For jhāna: Pradeepika 'එළඹ බැලීම්' (closely looking, P L73), Margaya 'special effort in taking the object' (M L164). For magga: Pradeepika 'එතර කරවීම්' (crossing over, P L75), Margaya 'the power of leading to good destinations, bad destinations and nibbāna', and its list of nine path factors includes view (දිට්ඨි) generally (M L172–L174). Do not merge these.

Margaya states that atthi = avigata and natthi = vigata in both dhamma and power, and are repeated for listeners' benefit (M L200). Pradeepika's part 1 glosses the four differently (present, absent, disappearing, not disappearing; P L81–L87). Check later parts for Pradeepika's own position.

No Abhidharma Margaya lines fall in this part (Margaya L1–210 is read in part 1). Conditions 3–6 therefore cannot be compared side by side here; the merge step should check whether and how the Margaya treats adhipati, anantara, samanantara and sahajāta.

Within the Pradeepika, the Pāli sentences quoted for each case (e.g. 'kusalā dhammā kusalassa dhammassa adhipatipaccayena paccayo' [C082-P:L1781]) appear to come from the Paṭṭhāna's analytical sections, but this part never names its Pāli source. The attribution needs an expert check.

Internal difference: the object-predominance table lists what supports greed-rooted cittas as worldly wholesome 17, worldly resultant 31, greed-rooted 8 and desirable matter 18 [C082-P:L1702–L1707]. The 10th vīthi adds 20 functional (kiriyā) cittas and 35 cetasikas [C082-P:L2183–L2193]. The overall paccaya list of 84 cittas [C082-P:L1660] would include kiriyā.

Mutuality: the Pradeepika (P) gives the leaning-sticks image and says not all co-arising states are mutual [C082-P:L3346]. The Margaya (M) defines it plainly as 'helping and being helped in return', lists the same three sets (mind and mental factors, the four great elements, rebirth mind-aggregates with the heart-base), and uses no image [C082-M:L92].

Support: M uses a different image, paper supporting a painting [C082-M:L96], where P describes support as 'a place to stand' [C082-P:L3616]. Both split prenascent support into base-prenascent and base-object-prenascent. M explicitly omits base-object-prenascent support as too hard to grasp [C082-M:L100]. P explains it at length, including the last heart-base near death [C082-P:L3624–L3630].

Decisive support: both give the same three kinds. M defines object decisive support as 'an object the world regards as good' [C082-M:L106]. P speaks of objects 'to be honoured' and shows the same honoured object supporting both wholesome and unwholesome states [C082-P:L4347–L4353]. M's natural decisive support explicitly includes 'pleasure and pain' [C082-M:L110], which matches P's bodily pleasure/pain, weather, food and lodging examples [C082-P:L5493–L5551]. The nine-mode worked examples appear only in P.
The M lines cited here were read only as a spot-check. Part 1 covers M in full, and its readings should take precedence at merge.
Only the Pradeepika (C082-P) is assigned to this part. The Margaya (M L1–210) belongs to part 1, so no side-by-side comparison can be made here.

Within the Pradeepika itself, prenascence is first divided into two kinds (object and base) [C082-P:L5729], but a third label, 'වස්ත්වාරම්මණ පුරේජාත' (the heart base taken as object near death), is added afterwards [C082-P:L5739]. The merge step should check whether the Margaya uses the same division.

The Pradeepika uses the same frame for every condition in this range: 'ත්‍රිරාශිය' (conditioning / conditioned / excluded states), then 'විසජ්ජනා වාර හෙවත් වීථි' with Pāli sentences and a Sinhala gloss. The merge step should check whether the other parts and the Margaya use the same terms.

This part covers only Pradeepika L7370–9073. Abhidharma Margaya (M L1–210) is covered by part 1, so any comparison of how Margaya treats conditions 17–24 and the summary table must come from that part or the merge step.

Within Pradeepika the later conditions are defined largely by cross-reference: dissociation kinds 2–4 point back to the base-prenascent support, object-and-base prenascent support and postnascent conditions (L7998–L8002); the seven kinds of presence point back to conasence, support, prenascence, postnascence, material nutriment and life-faculty (L8250–L8264); absence equals proximity (L8916), disappearance equals absence (L9022–L9028) and non-disappearance equals presence (L9032–L9034). The merge step should check these against the earlier parts' readings of those conditions.
uncertainties: Numbering mismatch in Pradeepika's object-condition patterns: the headings run 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, then '3. වීථිය' at P L1137 (unwholesome → indeterminate), then 7, 8, 9. Given the stated total of nine (P L520), the L1137 heading is presumably 6. Not corrected here.
P L224 (root condition, pattern 2) says the triple-rooted mind has 'අදෙෂ, අමොහ යන හේතු තුන' but names only two roots. අලොභ appears to be omitted.

P L1254 says 'ශක්ති අටෙන්' (of eight powers) but lists nine items, with 'ආරම්මණ පුරෙජාත' appearing twice. 'ව්‍යාරම්මණ-නිස්සය / ව්‍යාරම්මණ විප්පයුත්ත' is probably OCR for vatthārammaṇa (වත්ථාරම්මණ). Compare the cleaner list at P L1461.

OCR and spelling problems in P: 'අවලොස්' for අටළොස් (L143); 'පටිස' for පටිඝ (L1009, L1210); 'වෙෂ/දෙෂ/වෙදෂ' alternations for ද්වේෂ (L115 ff.); 'කුලභිඥවට' for කුසලාභිඥවට (L1579); missing opening parentheses at L993, L1412, L1481.

P L401 speaks of 'එකට ගැටෙන ප්‍රත්‍යය දෙළොසක්' (twelve co-occurring conditions) for the root condition. This matches the maximum of 12 at L391, but the per-pattern counts vary (10, 9, 8, 7, 6, 5, 12, 10). Doctrinal check advised.

P L1346 says an arahant's insight takes '32 resultant consciousnesses', while L1418 and L1422 speak of 36 for the direct-knowledge objects. Possibly intentional (supramundane results excluded), but needs expert check.
M L104 opens upanissaya with 'නිශ්ශ්‍රය ප්‍රත්‍යය තුන් ආකාර වේ'. The context shows it should be upanissaya (උපනිශ්ශ්‍රය). This looks like a typo.
M L100 says the vatthārammaṇa-purejāta form is 'hard to understand and so not shown', yet M L116 and L192 refer to it as though defined.
M L74 'දෙපනස් සාධිපති ජජවනය' is garbled (probably 'දෙපනස් සාධිපති ජවනය'), and the Pali list at M L13 has vowel-sign OCR variants (පච්චයේ for පච්චයෝ).
M L128 (āsevana) excludes the last javana and fruition javana and counts 47 mundane javanas. Pradeepika's treatment falls in a later part, so compare there.
Pradeepika's account of the six-coloured rays in the fourth week (P L35) is traditional and devotional. It should not be treated as a historical claim.

Part boundary: this part ends at P L1634, in the middle of the 9th object-condition pattern (indeterminate → unwholesome). The remaining 22 conditions in Pradeepika are covered by parts 2–5. Margaya was read in full here.
L1798 gives the conditioned cetasikas as 'විරති අප්‍රමාණ්‍ය හැර චෛතසික තෙවිස්සය' (23), but the same exclusion at L1914 gives 'තෙතිසය' (33). 38 − 5 = 33, so L1798 is probably a misprint.
L1862 counts mahaggata and lokuttara wholesome cittas as 'සතලොසය' (17), but 9 mahaggata + 4 path = 13. L1948/L1960 total 21 (8+9+4). This is a numbering mismatch; do not correct it silently.
L1702–L1715 (object-predominance table) omits functional (kiriyā) cittas as a support for greed-rooted cittas, while L2189 includes 'ක්‍රියා සිත් විස්සය'. These are inconsistent within the source.
L2145 looks garbled: 'ආරම්මණ, ආරම්මණාධිපති, ප්‍රත්‍යය ශක්තියම ලැබේ' seems to have lost 'ආරම්මණූපනිස්සය' and the phrase naming which force applies (compare L1800, L1916).

L2453 lists five co-occurring forces for unwholesome→unwholesome anantara (anantara, samanantara, āsevana, natthi, vigata) and omits upanissaya, which appears in the wholesome and indeterminate cases (L2292, L2512, L2636, L2660). This may be an omission; it needs an expert check.
L2596 speaks of 'පඤ්චවොකාර භවාඞ්ගුපච්ඡේද එකුන්විස්ස' (19), whereas the table at L2520 gives 15 for pañcavokāra and 4 for arūpa (L2521). This is a numbering mismatch.
L2768 glosses the samanantara 5th-vīthi Pāli (vipāka/kiriyā abyākata → vipāka/kiriyā abyākata) as '...පශ්චිම පශ්චිම වූ අකුසල ස්කන්ධයන්ට'. 'අකුසල' contradicts the Pāli and looks like a gloss error.

L2924 lists 'සම්පයුත්ත' among the forces co-occurring when wholesome mind supports mind-born matter. Association normally holds only between mental states, so 'විප්පයුත්ත' may be intended. This needs an expert check.
L2834 omits pavatti-kammaja matter from the great-element paccaya list, while L3142 includes 'ප්‍රවෘත්ති කර්මජ රූපයෝ'. This is a minor internal inconsistency.

Probable OCR/typographic forms: 'වීය්‍යීය' (L1749) for විරිය; 'විහේතුක' (L2574) probably for ද්විහේතුක/දුහේතුක; recurring 'මනොවාරාවජ්ජන' for මනොද්වාරාවජ්ජන and 'භවාඞ්ග වලන' for භවාඞ්ග චලන; unbalanced parentheses (e.g. no opening one at L1842, no closing one at L2320). The '(2)' count at L2581 is ambiguous for a row that lists 4 + 2 rebirth-linkings.

L2672 says anantara and samanantara share identical conditioning and conditioned states and glosses 'sama' only as 'මනාකොට'. This part gives no further account of how the two conditions differ. The merge step should check parts 1 and 3–5.

L2226 wording on the non-percipient case ('දෙවන ජාතියෙහි අසංඥ භවයෙහි උපදනා පුද්ගලයාගේ චුති චිත්තය') is compressed. It reads as the death-moment before non-percipient rebirth supporting the rebirth-linking 500 great aeons later, but the grammar should be checked.

L1866 says a wholesome citta has 'three or four' predominant factors but does not say which cittas have three. Do not infer (for example, a link to knowledge-dissociated cittas) without an expert check.
This part starts at condition 3 (L1635) and ends inside condition 6 at L3343, after the 9th sahajāta vīthi. The page marker pdf:312/printed:301 at L3342 means the next condition begins in part 3.

At P L4029–L4031 the Pali reads 'ඛන්ධා වත්ථුස්ස' (aggregates → heart-base), but the Sinhala gloss says the heart-base supports the aggregates, which is the reverse direction. This is a text or gloss mismatch and has not been resolved.
The support (nissaya) list jumps from item 7 to item 9 with no item 8 (editorial note at P L4037). The item may be missing from the print. It has not been reconstructed.
In the decisive-support list, items are numbered 2, 4, 4, 5… with no 3 (editorial note at P L4593). The content seems complete, and the numbering is left as printed.

At P L3792 (wholesome → mind-born matter, support condition), the forces listed include සම්පයුත්ත (association), where විප්පයුත්ත (dissociation) would be expected for mind supporting matter. This needs an expert check.

Rebirth-mind counts differ: 'ප්‍රතිසන්ධි සිත් පසළොසය' (15) at P L3511 and 'එකුන් විස්සය' (19) at P L3965. This is probably because the first context includes the heart-base (five-aggregate existence only) and the second covers all rebirths. It needs confirmation.

Recurring OCR or spelling forms: 'වෙෂ' for ද්වේෂ throughout; 'ප්‍රත්‍යාක්පන්න' for ප්‍රත්‍යොත්පන්න (P L5305, L5379, L5443, L5573); 'සංස' for සංඝ (e.g. P L5143, L5255); 'රුහිතුප්පාද' for lohituppāda (P L5249); 'පරිසිට්ඨි' for පරියිට්ඨි (P L5399). These were not corrected in the citations.
M L104 says 'නිශ්ශ්‍රය ප්‍රත්‍යය තුන් ආකාර වේ' (support has three kinds), which is almost certainly a slip for උපනිශ්ශ්‍රය (decisive support). Part 1 should confirm.

P L5319–L5321 says lust can decisively support even developing the path and higher attainments (as motivation to overcome lust). This is doctrinally subtle and should be checked by an expert before anyone paraphrases it on screen.

The claims that the five gravest acts and fixed wrong view certainly lead to hell in the next life (P L5285, L5289) are presented as doctrine. They need careful handling and expert framing if referenced at all.

L6447 and L6461: the text speaks of the '21 wholesome cittas' but gives the number of their volitions as 'එකුන් විස්සය' (19). L6477 gives 'චෙතනා එක්විස්සය' (21), so this is probably a misprint. Not corrected.

L7190: the list of co-arising conditions for wholesome faculties supporting mind-born matter includes 'අඤ්ඤමඤ්ඤ' (mutuality), while the parallel kamma and nutriment lists for mind-born matter (L6483, L6966) do not. This needs an expert check.

Scope: this part begins at condition 10 (L5721) and ends inside condition 16, faculty (last item at L7364–L7366). Condition 17, jhāna, starts at L7370 (part 5). The enumerated counts (47 and 51 impulsions, 33 past volitions, 85 cittas for postnascence, and so on) were not checked against the citta tables in other chapters.

L7372 names seven absorption factors (with pleasant, unpleasant and neutral feeling listed separately), while the three-heap list at L7386 gives five (feeling counted once). This is probably a difference of counting, not a contradiction, but it needs expert confirmation.

L7919 says 'seven' co-occurring conditions for the indeterminate association case but lists only six (non-disappearance/avigata appears to be missing). This is a numbering mismatch; do not fill it in.

L7781 and L7807 describe the path factors in resultant and functional (indeterminate) minds as 'කුසල මාර්ගාඞ්ගයෝ අටදෙන'. This probably means the 'right' set of eight, not literally wholesome states, and needs an expert check.
L8472 reads 'විපාක සිත් සත්සය' where L8476 and similar passages have 'සතිසය' (36). Likely an OCR or print slip.
L8514 gives the rebirth minds as 'පසළොස' (15, five-aggregate existence) where L8480 gives 'එකුන් විස්සය' (19); the change of context may explain this, but it needs checking.
The presence condition's answer-sections are misnumbered: after the 9th comes '12.' (L8732), then 11, 12, 13 (an editorial note at L8730 records this). A '10.' is missing from the sequence.

At L8112/L8178 the dissociation prenascent case lists 22 resultant minds, while L8116 gives 32. This is probably explained by whether the ten sense consciousnesses are included; also, the gloss at L8178 omits the 20 functional minds even though the Pali line names them. Needs expert check.

The seven disappearance answer-sections and thirteen non-disappearance answer-sections are not printed; the reader is told to substitute the term in the absence and presence sections (L9028, L9034). They cannot be verified independently here.

The summary table (L9048–L9073) is a transcription of stacked printed headings and +/– marks (see the editorial comment at L9040–L9046). Individual cells (e.g. nutriment '–' but kamma '+' for one-aggregate existence) should be checked against the printed page before being quoted.
Several parentheses are opened but not closed in the transcription (e.g. L7480, L8306, L8740). These are transcription artefacts with no effect on meaning.

According to the file frontmatter, the extract contains only the Sinhala commentary, not the Pali root text, so the Pali formulae quoted inline are the author's citations and have not been checked against the Paṭṭhāna itself.
